body_markdown:
## **What teams say when they choose us, in their own words**


We have thousands of recorded evaluation calls, so instead of guessing why teams pick Storylane, I read what buyers actually said. Five questions: why they choose us, what they actually use us for, why the AI and platform direction matters to them, why they pick us over the alternatives, and, because the honest version includes it, when we're not the right fit. Storylane is no longer just interactive demos, it's a platform that now includes RepX, our AI sales agent, and buyers are increasingly evaluating it that way.


## **The short version**


- **Ease of use is the #1 reason teams pick Storylane (51% of evaluations).** Buyers want their AEs to run demos without an engineer on the call.
- **The most common job is in the sales cycle, not marketing.** Teams hire Storylane first to standardize demos, arm reps with leave-behinds, and qualify inbound, then marketing and CS uses follow. It usually lands in one team and spreads across the GTM org.
- **Buyers are choosing an AI-first, multi-product platform.** AI capture and editing, a native MCP / Claude connector, and RepX (our AI sales agent) come up again and again as the reason teams feel Storylane is "ahead of the curve."
- **Navattic is the most common head-to-head (raised in ~1 in 4 evaluations).** Buyers choose Storylane on UX, editing depth, AI, and pricing.
- **When buyers go a different direction, it's usually about fit, not a flaw:** budget, a lighter need, or a product and motion that isn't demo-led yet.


## **How I ran this**


Sybill has catalogued 4,300+ external conversations. For the frequencies below I coded a deduplicated set of ~90 unique new-business evaluations (one primary call per account); quotes and platform themes draw on a deeper read of ~240 recent calls and named customer interviews. Calls span the full platform, interactive demos and RepX. Quotes are anonymized to role and company type unless the customer is a public reference. This is our own pipeline, so it's why buyers pick *us* , and it's correlational, not a controlled test.

Ease of use wins, and it's specific: buyers want the people closest to the deal to build and run demos themselves. The moment it clicks is often watching a rep do it live.


> "I was really impressed that the AE was doing the demos himself. That told me it wasn't hard to use, and that was the motion I wanted to push on our team." — VP of Sales Enablement, enterprise SaaS


But knowing why teams pick Storylane raises the next question: what do they actually use it for?


## **2. What teams use Storylane for**


It's easy to assume a demo platform is a marketing tool. When I coded the same calls for the job teams were hiring Storylane to do, the pattern cut in a couple of ways: the most common use cases live in the sales cycle, not just at the top of the funnel.

Three clusters, ordered by how often they came up:


**In the sales cycle (most common).** AEs and SEs reach for Storylane to standardize the demo so every rep delivers the same quality, to send personalized leave-behinds after a call, to qualify inbound with RepX, and to replace live demos that are heavy to run. The recurring driver is consistency: taking demo quality off the shoulders of the strongest rep and making it the floor for the whole team.


> "It's a priority for me to build a demo environment and process that's consistent across the board and removes that barrier for our salesforce." — Product and strategy leader, SaaS


**At the top of the funnel (very common).** Marketing embeds interactive tours on the website and landing pages, runs them at events and in campaigns, and uses them to capture and qualify leads. Buyers describe it as a lightweight preview that lets a modern buyer self-serve before they'll take a call.


> "We want to be able to say, 'don't believe us, come check this out.' Just to see, hey, this is a real product, this is what the data looks like." — Product leader, SaaS


**After the sale (growing).** CS teams use Storylane for onboarding, customer education, and showing off new features, a way to scale walkthroughs without getting on a call with every account.


> "This is part of customer onboarding. It's going to drive platform engagement for users, which is a huge piece for us going forward." — Sales and strategy lead, analytics


The through-line, and the pattern worth the most attention: **Storylane usually lands in one team and spreads.** An account starts with a single job, often a marketing tour or a landing-page embed, and then sales, pre-sales, and CS see the output and want their own access. It shows up two ways: seat counts grow past the initial pilot, and new teams adopt it for their own use cases.

**Takeaway:** the strongest early foothold is often marketing, but the durable value is a platform the whole GTM org runs on. Sell the first job, then make the second team's access one conversation away.


## **3. Buyers are betting on an AI-first, multi-product platform**


The AI capability isn't a checkbox for these buyers, it's often the deciding factor. Teams describe Storylane as future-ready: AI that builds the first draft of a demo, an AI editor that reworks it in bulk, a native MCP / Claude connector, and RepX carrying the same intelligence into live buyer conversations.


Phenom, an applied-AI HR company, built 35 interactive demos in three weeks for a flagship event, and it was the AI that made it possible.


> "The thing that really drew us to you was your innovation, the way you're applying AI and automation to help build out those story narratives. That's what allowed us to scale, to build all these demos in such a quick amount of time." — Mike, Product Marketing, Phenom


The AI editor comes up as a day-to-day time-saver, and the MCP / Claude connector as a sign of where the product is heading.


> "The ability to use the AI editor to bulk update variables like a graph or table has been a game changer for our demo creation." — Product Manager, software company


> "We're looking for a solution that leverages AI agents like Claude, trained on our product documentation. That's exactly what we need to scale." — VP of Sales, cybersecurity company


And increasingly, buyers evaluate RepX, our AI sales agent, as part of the same platform, not a separate tool. What lands is that it's an actual agent, not a chatbot.


> "What I love about RepX is that it's not just a reactive chatbot. It's an AI sales agent that qualifies visitors, asks follow-up questions, and routes them to our calendar. It's a completely different motion." — Director of Marketing, B2B SaaS


> "An agent that can handle 20 conversations at once, even at 10 PM on a Saturday, is exactly why we see RepX as a differentiator." — Head of Sales Operations, tech platform


The through-line is a platform that keeps working after the demo is built.


> "Storylane feels ahead of the curve. While others are just static screenshots, we're moving toward a truly interactive, future-ready motion where the demo is always working for us." — GTM Strategist, B2B SaaS


And once a team is in, the platform tends to spread. Phenom again:


> "Other teams were interested. Product partners were like, you've got to get my teams access to this tool. Multiple teams see the value." — Mike, Product Marketing, Phenom


**Takeaway:** buyers aren't just buying a demo builder. They're buying into an AI-first platform, demos, an AI editor, an MCP/Claude connector, and RepX, that they expect to keep paying off as their GTM motion gets more automated.

The recurring wedge is editability, and increasingly, AI. Video-based tools can't keep up with a changing product, and older interactive tools aren't moving as fast on AI.


> "The UX is just way easier than Navattic, with even more editing capabilities. That was really our primary thing. She's tested it and we're moving forward." — Head of ABM, B2B SaaS (switching from Navattic)


Two structural advantages come up as tie-breakers: **unlimited viewer licenses** (pay for creators, not viewers) and **migration tooling** that strips guides from a competitor's demos, lowering the cost of switching.


**Takeaway:** the win pattern is editability + ease of use + AI + pricing. When a buyer is coming from video, lead with "your product changes; your demos shouldn't have to be rebuilt."


## **5. When Storylane isn't the right fit**


No tool wins every deal, and the honest reasons buyers go a different direction are rarely dramatic. Setting aside standard enterprise due diligence (security and compliance reviews, a normal step rather than a reason deals fall through), three patterns explain most of it: budget, a lighter need, and product or motion fit.


**Budget and timing.** Pricing is the single most common hesitation, raised in about 1 in 3 evaluations, but it's usually about stage and timing, not sticker shock, and it shows up in won deals too.


> "We're in the early stages of building our GTM motion. With a limited budget, we're prioritizing core infrastructure over advanced marketing tools this cycle." — CRO, early-stage software company


**A lighter or different need.** Some teams just want a simple recorder for a few leave-behinds and don't need a full platform yet.


> "We really just need something to record and track simple leave-behind demos. I don't think we need all the advanced editing or interactive features." — Head of Product, mid-market SaaS


**Product or motion fit.** Some products are harder to capture, and some teams aren't demo-led yet, very lean or pre-GTM, so a dedicated platform isn't the right investment at that moment.


> "Our team is three people. We're focused on immediate product development, and our sales motion isn't quite at the point where we need a dedicated interactive platform yet." — Lead engineer, early-stage startup


**Takeaway:** the through-line is fit and timing, not a flaw. The buyers who don't move forward are usually early-stage, light-need, or not-yet-demo-led, and many come back when they are.
